text.p: A recent survey of small businesses shows them mostly optimistic for this year, but a closer look at problems they face and another study focusing on the most-frustrating problems of owners leaving their much-bigger businesses reveals daunting challenges.

Both groups put employee issues at the top of their frustration lists. They range from finding qualified employees and providing them with benefits, to illegitimate claims for worker's compensation and other workplace problems such as sexual harassment, wrongful termination and employee theft.

Dun & Bradstreet, the provider of commercial credit and business marketing information, recently surveyed 398 owners of small businesses in the manufacturing, services and wholesale industries. Ninety-eight of the businesses were owned by women, and 59 by minorities.

Their responses, coming from people whose businesses are relatively young, are enlightening for the prospective business owner, especially when compared with responses from 606 veteran business owners in a second survey done by The Geneva Companies. The Irvine, Calif.-based company, which specialises in evaluating and selling privately held, middle-market businesses valued up to $150 million, aimed its survey at owners considering leaving their businesses.

"Many of these business owners now have begun the process of exiting their businesses because the joy of owning a business no longer is what it once was to them," said David Troob, Geneva's chairman. "Some may have become burned out and are weary of the rigours of business ownership," he added.

It may be that those owners have simply reached the stage in their personal and business lives that they are ready to bow out. But with so many veteran and new business owners citing similar problems, it is cause for concern.

Ninety percent of the companies in the D&B survey have 20 or fewer employees. Most operate in only one location and recorded less than $500,000 in annual revenues. Businesses with five or fewer employees accounted for 70 percent of the total, and half said they use part-time help.
Nearly half of the business owners said finding qualified employees was a key issue for them.

"The type of business we're in requires us to practically start from scratch when we hire a new employee," said Jim Vihonsky, owner of Creative Building Supply and Sheet Metal, in Lakewood, N.J.. The company has 11 full-time and one part-time employee.

"It takes a great deal of learning, especially in the math field, for a salesman to really start being a benefit to us," he said. "It's simple mathematics, to be able to work with the computers and calculate, and be able to think while they're on the phone with a customer."

Vihonsky said it usually takes six months to a year of training before he is satisfied with the performance of a new salesperson. "Every once in a while you stumble across somebody who is able to pick it up," he said. "Once you get them, you want to keep them."
Toward that end, the firm offers healthcare benefits and a pension plan.

Proflex of Texas Inc., a Houston manufacturer of insulated flexible air ducts and central heating and air conditioning parts for sale to wholesalers, also cited employee issues as its main challenge. Most of its shopworkers are minimum-wage day labourers.

"In our industry, there's not a lot of experience needed. Once the charts are made for each person at each table, it's basically 'look at the number, look at what you're doing and use common sense.' But you don't always find that," said Sabrina Atkinson, who is responsible for day-to-day operations at the firm, which employs 20 people.

"Some people don't take their job as seriously as you would think they would. Sometimes people don't care," said Atkinson. "I get one excuse after another why people can't work. I've had some who don't show up for two days and then tell me they want to work. I tell them I'm sorry, I already hired somebody else.
"I can't run a business depending on their schedule, their availability or their not being in jail," she said.
More than 40 percent of the small business owners said managing rising insurance costs and dealing with government regulations and taxes were among their toughest challenges.

While they may not be much different from their larger corporate cousins in that respect, the small business owner filling numerous roles has to be a specialist in each, or at least know when to seek expert help.
Nearly half of the small businesses provide employee healthcare benefits, D&B said, with most reporting that their health insurance costs had either increased or held steady.
To manage the higher cost of insurance, 37 percent said they had shopped for a new carrier in 1996, and 41 percent said they assumed the extra cost without passing it on to their employees.
Atkinson said her company extends health coverage after one year of employment. But it does not provide retirement benefits.

Vihonsky doesn't mind paying for health and retirement benefits to keep his employees. But like others who cited state and federal workplace regulations, what does irk him is having to pay what he sees as unreasonably high workers' compensation insurance rates.

"We've been in business going on 5 years, and we have not had one claim in all that time," he said. "I have to pay 8.9 percent for a truck driver -- why am I paying such high insurance on the vehicle? It's things like that that infuriate me."
